Welcome to the StarMade Guides! This is a replica of the in-game documentation built by the community to help players get started in StarMade. The old documentation can be found here, but is not maintained. For the most up to date information please refer to this site or to the in-game guides. Click on the Introduction to get started.
StarMade has two distinct AI systems: ship/turret AI controlled by the AI Module block, and AI Crew — NPC companions you can hire and command.
A fleet is a group of AI-controlled ships that act together under a single set of orders. No special block is required — fleets are created and managed entirely through the Fleet Panel (K).

Build mode has a radial menu of shape tools for placing blocks in geometric patterns, and an advanced build mode panel full of power tools. Together they dramatically speed up construction of large ships and stations.

StarMade uses a rail-based docking system. A ship docks to rail blocks on a station or another ship with a Rail Docker block. Rails handle fixed docking, turrets, moving platforms and elevators, cargo transfer, and automatic hangar docking.
A ship core makes no power of its own. Without a reactor your thrusters run at only 5% of their strength and weapons, shields and other systems don't work, so every real ship needs a reactor.

Shipyards are Space Station based systems that allow players to design ships in a temporary virtual creative environment and mass produce those designs from a loaded design, which is similar to a blueprint. You can also dock an existing ship into a shipyard to completely deconstruct it, or repair it using an existing loaded design.
All key bindings can be remapped in the game settings. The defaults listed here are the standard layout. Panel keys (inventory, map, catalog and so on) are listed in HUD & Interface.
Your character moves in two very different ways: walking where there is gravity, and floating freely in zero gravity.
The HUD (Heads-Up Display) gives you live information about your character and ship at a glance.

StarMade is a voxel-based space sandbox game. You explore a procedurally generated universe, build ships and stations block by block, gather resources, craft items, fight enemies, and team up with other players.
StarMade has a fully integrated, Turing-complete logic system. You can build anything from a simple light switch to a fully functional CPU using logic blocks connected to each other.
Building on the basics of activation blocks and connections, StarMade provides four additional logic blocks that let you build complex circuits.
StarMade's crafting system is divided into three basic stages: refining, component manufacturing, and block assembly.
Production or 'crafting' in StarMade is primarily achieved via various types of Factories. A full production line requires multiple linked factories.
The Catalog stores ship blueprints — saved snapshots of ships and stations that can be purchased and spawned elsewhere.
Factions let players group together, protect their ships and stations, declare wars, and organise with ranks and permissions.
Understanding armor and damage types is essential for both building durable ships and designing effective weapons.
Ships are built block by block in Build Mode. This guide takes you through spawning your first ship and making it flight-ready.

Chambers are special blocks that plug into your reactor to give your ship additional capabilities — jump drives, stealth, enhanced mobility, and more. They are the primary way to unlock advanced ship systems.
Every ship needs a power reactor to run its systems. This guide covers how to build and balance your reactor.
Salvagers function similarly to weapons, but without secondaries or effects. Salvage systems are used to mine ores from asteroids, and to salvage overheating shipwrecks and abandoned stations.
Shields are your ship's first layer of defence. All incoming damage hits shields before reaching your hull and blocks. When shields are depleted they enter a Shield Outage before recharging.
A ship, station turret or docked entity with a BOBBY AI Module can fly and fight on its own. Only one AI Module is allowed per ship.
A ship is the primary way to travel through space, fight enemies, and carry cargo. Every ship is built around a Ship Core block — the single block that defines the ship.
StarMade uses a block-group system to determine how sets of same-type blocks behave together. This is most important for weapons, where grouping affects how shots are fired.

Thrusters are modules that allow you to move your ship, and consume energy from your Reactor in order to do so. Thrusters have a linear power consumption per module, but diminishing returns on how much thrust each thruster module on a ship produces. Larger ships will require more thrusters and more power to move at the same speed as a smaller ship.

StarMade has three primary weapon types, three utility weapons, and explosive warhead blocks. Primary weapons can be linked to a secondary weapon to alter the functions and stats of the primary weapon, and can be linked to an effect system to alter its damage type distribution.

StarMade Galaxy is a new version of StarMade built in Unity SRP that one of the developers of the original game is working on in their free time. This version of the game is publicly unavailable as of the time of writing, however you can support Schema via Patreon to gain access to the experimental branch of StarMade Galaxy, but there is currently no build yet. Note that this is completely optional, and that the official Java version is still maintained and widely used throughout the community. If you're new to StarMade the suggestion remains to stick to the Java version from Steam or the official StarMade site. There is a teaser trailer of StarMade Galaxy available on YouTube.

The StarMade universe is vast. Understanding its structure and using the navigation tools efficiently will save you a lot of time.
Raw resources are the foundation of everything you build. There are four families of raw materials, each found in different places across the universe.

StarMade has two distinct AI systems: ship/turret AI controlled by the AI Module block, and AI Crew — NPC companions you can hire and command.
See Ship & Turret AI.
AI Crew are NPC characters you can hire and give direct commands to.

Crew is hired from Advanced Shops — these are special NPC stations found: In the starting sector of new worlds Rarely throughout the universe (check the navigation panel for Trading Guild NPCs) Talk to the NPC at an advanced shop (R) to hire up to 5 active crew members. You can have more total crew by assigning some to a ship as their home base.

Press the AI Control key (default: check your key bindings — listed in the HUD as AI Control) to open the crew command panel. Select a crew member from the list on the left and issue commands. Command Effect Follow me Crew member follows your character Wait here Crew member stays at current location Go to point Crew member moves to a position you designate

Crew members have a home — a ship or station they belong to. By default they spawn near where you hired them. To reassign a crew member to your ship: Tell the crew member to Follow You. Go to your ship. Tell the crew member to Go to a Point on your ship. The ship is now their home and they will move with it when it travels.
documents.s: Assigning Crew to a Ship (Setting Home)

documents.t: Press the AI Config Panel key (check key bindings) to open the full crew panel. In the Crew tab you can: Rename crew members Remove crew members Adjust individual behaviour settings

You can only have 5 crew members under direct active command at a time. Crew assigned to a ship as their home do not count against this limit while they are stationed there. Discharge crew to their ship to free up active command slots.
A fleet is a group of AI-controlled ships that act together under a single set of orders. No special block is required — fleets are created and managed entirely through the Fleet Panel (K).
Open the Fleet Panel (K). Create a new fleet and give it a name. Add ships to the fleet by selecting them from your faction's ship list. The first ship added becomes the flagship.

The flagship is the anchor of the fleet. It determines: The reference position for all formation modes. The shared target in combined targeting mode. The recall destination for carrier operations. If the flagship is removed from the fleet, the next ship in the list automatically takes over as the new flagship.

When creating a fleet you assign it a type, which describes its intended role. This is a classification label and does not restrict which commands you can issue. Type Intended Role Assault Front-line combat Defense Sector or station guarding Scouting Exploration and reconnaissance Supporting Logistics, repair, escort Cargo Hauling goods between locations Commerce Trade operations Mining Asteroid mining operations Salvage Wreck salvage operations
Issue commands from the Fleet Panel. Commands are grouped below by function.

Command Behaviour Idle Fleet holds position and ignores enemies Move Fleet moves to the specified sector Patrol Fleet patrols a route between two or more waypoint sectors Escort Fleet follows the flagship; attacks enemies within 1 sector radius of it

Command Behaviour Attack Fleet moves to target sector and engages enemy ships Defend Fleet moves to sector and attacks nearby enemies; will not chase more than 2 sectors Sentry Fleet stays in place and attacks enemies that come into range Standoff Fleet engages at distance and retreats if enemies close in Repair Fleet disengages combat and prioritises repairs

Command Behaviour Mine All non-flagship ships mine asteroids in the current sector Carrier Recall All ships return to the pickup rails of the last carrier they docked with Activate Remote Triggers a named inner-ship logic remote on every fleet member

Command Behaviour Cloak / Uncloak All capable ships engage or disengage cloaking Jam / Unjam All capable ships enable or disable radar jamming Interdict / Stop Interdict All capable ships enable or disable FTL interdiction

Command Behaviour Trade (NPC) Fleet moves to fulfill a trade order between two locations Trade (Active) Fleet actively seeks trade runs Trade (Waiting) Fleet waits at faction homebase to fulfill incoming trade orders

Two formation commands keep ships in organised positions relative to the flagship: Formation Behaviour Sentry Formation Holds formation while idle; if enemies are spotted, ships will break out of formation and attack. Idle Formation Holds formation without engaging enemies While ships cannot currently engage enemies and remain in formation, the Idle in Formation command can be useful in combat for regrouping a scattered fleet. Warning: Formation modes are experimental and can cause movement glitches, especially with large ships or crowded sectors. Use with caution.

Each fleet has a combat engagement setting that controls unprompted aggression: Setting Behaviour Sometimes Engage (default) Fleet engages enemies opportunistically Always Engage Fleet attacks all enemies on sight Never Engage Fleet ignores all enemies unless commanded

When combined targeting is enabled, all fleet members share the flagship's current target. Every ship in the fleet focuses fire on the same enemy, updated every second. This is effective for quickly destroying individual targets but leaves other nearby threats unaddressed.

If your fleet ships were launched from a carrier using the Pickup Rail system, each ship remembers its last docking point. Issue the Carrier Recall command to send them all back to their pickup rails automatically. Ships navigate back individually and re-dock when they arrive. The process completes once all ships are docked. Recall only works if the ship has docked to a pickup rail at least once. Ships spawned fresh without a prior docking have no recall point.

Build mode has a radial menu of shape tools for placing blocks in geometric patterns, and an advanced build mode panel full of power tools. Together they dramatically speed up construction of large ships and stations.

You must be in Build Mode (inside a ship core or build block). Hold Left Ctrl to enter advanced build mode; the tool panel appears on the right side of the screen. Tap Left Ctrl twice to make it stick, and tap it again to leave. In advanced build mode: You aim with the mouse cursor instead of the centre of the screen. The mouse wheel rotates the selected block. The build size sliders apply, so one click can place or remove a whole area of blocks. The middle mouse button puts the block you are pointing at on your hotbar. Speed tip: Hold Left Shift in build mode to move much faster — essential for working on large structures.

Press the backtick key (`) in Build Mode to open the radial menu of eight shape tools. Pick one from the ring, then click in the world to use it. How clicks work for every shape tool: Normally each click lands on a point 5 blocks in front of your camera, so you can build out into empty space. Hold Left Ctrl to click exactly on the block face under your cursor instead. Left-click starts a shape that places blocks; right-click starts one that removes them. The first click decides which. Removing needs you to click on actual blocks. A live preview shows the shape: yellow to place, red to remove. Press Escape to cancel a shape you have started. A finished shape is one undo step (Ctrl+Z). Shapes use your symmetry planes, remove filter and build size, and you need enough blocks in your inventory. The centre button of the radial menu toggles Hollow Mode: Box, Circle, Cylinder, Ellipsoid and Polygon are then built as empty shells or outlines instead of solid fills.
The default mode. Place or remove one block (or one build-size area) per click.

Draw a straight line of blocks. Click to set the start point. Click again to set the end point. The line is placed. Left Ctrl + mouse wheel cycles axis restriction: Auto, XY plane, XZ plane, YZ plane. Hold Left Shift to snap to straight lines and 45° diagonals.
Fill a rectangular volume with blocks. Click to set the first corner. Click to set the opposite corner. The box is placed. Hollow mode builds only the six walls.

Draw a smooth curve. Click to set the start point. Click to set the end point. Click to set the control point. The curve bends toward it (it doesn't pass through it). Left Ctrl + mouse wheel cycles axis restriction. Hold Left Shift to snap angles.

Place a flat circle of blocks. Click to set the center. Click to set the radius. Left Ctrl + mouse wheel cycles the plane: Auto (facing you), XY, XZ, YZ. Hold Left Shift to snap the radius to 90° steps. Hollow mode builds a ring instead of a disc.

Build a cylinder. Click to set the base center. Click to set the radius. Click to set the height. While setting the radius, Left Ctrl + mouse wheel cycles the plane and Left Shift snaps it. Hollow mode builds an open tube with no ends.
Build a sphere or egg shape that fits inside a box. Click to set the first corner of the box. Click to set the opposite corner. The ellipsoid is placed. Hollow mode builds a shell one block thick.

Build a flat shape with 3 to 8 corners. Before you start, Left Ctrl + mouse wheel sets how many corners it has (3 by default). Click to place each corner. The shape is placed as soon as you place the last one. Hollow mode builds only the outline. The axis, plane and corner settings reset to their defaults after each shape.
Orientation: shows which way the selected block will face. Click it to pick a shape; the mouse wheel rotates the block. Undo / Redo: also Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y.

Three sliders (X, Y, Z) grow the area you place or remove with a single click. Scroll on a number to change it; right-click to reset it. The server sets the maximum (PLAYER_MAX_BUILD_AREA in server.cfg, 100 by default).

Click XY, XZ or YZ, then click a block to put a symmetry plane there. Placing or removing a block on one side does the same on the other side. Use all three planes to build in eight places at once. Unset removes a plane. ODD puts the plane through the middle of a block instead of between blocks — use it for ships with an odd width. Mirror cubic blocks / Mirror non-cubic blocks (both on by default) turn blocks on the other side so they mirror the ones you place, for example wedges and weapon outputs facing outward on both sides.

Copy Brush: click *PICK AREA*, then click the two corners of the area to copy. Cut Mode: with this on, copying an area also removes those blocks and puts them in your inventory, like a cut. Undo puts them back. Paste: shows the copy as a preview; click to place it. You need the blocks in your inventory. While pasting: Mouse wheel rotates the copy (hold Left Shift for the X axis, Left Ctrl for the Z axis). Left Alt + arrow keys / Page Up / Page Down nudge it one block (add Left Shift for 10). Links between blocks (C/V) are kept when both ends are inside the copied area. Templates: save a copy under a name with tags, and load it later in any build. Search by name or tag. Remove/Replace: pick a block type (from the list or Pick with camera). Right-click then only removes that type of block. Tick Only replace to swap those blocks for your selected block instead. This is invaluable for refitting ships. Highlight Selected in Entity: shows every block of the chosen type in the structure.
Save your hotbar as a named layout and load it again later.
Find a block by color: enter a hex color, pick a random one, or adjust saturation and brightness, then COPY TO HOTBAR.
Choose up to 10 blocks. With the mixer on, each block you place is picked at random from them — great for weathered or patterned hulls. SET FROM HOTBAR fills it from your hotbar.
Click Place Fill Origin and click a spot, then press Fill to flood the connected space (or the connected blocks of one type) with your selected block. The slider sets how many blocks each press adds.
Shows a guide shape in the world (line, circle, ellipsoid or torus) to build along. Tick Restrict Building to Helper to only place blocks inside it.
Create Docking builds a new docked entity in two clicks: pick the rail, then pick where its core goes and which way it faces. See Docking & Turrets.

Toggles that help while building: Buildlight: a flashlight for building in dark areas (also P). Lighten up blocks: removes shadows so dark interiors are fully lit. Turn it off now and then to see how your ship really looks. Structure info, extra block info, reactor convex hull, and center of mass indicators.

StarMade uses a rail-based docking system. A ship docks to rail blocks on a station or another ship with a Rail Docker block. Rails handle fixed docking, turrets, moving platforms and elevators, cargo transfer, and automatic hangar docking.

Block Role Rail Docker Goes on the ship being docked; the connector end Rail Basic Standard rail on the host. Docked ships move along it in the direction of its arrow Rail Turret Axis Lets the docked entity rotate around one axis; chain two for a full turret Rail Rotator Clock Wise / Counter Clock Wise Turns a docked entity as it passes over Rail Mass Enhancer Raises how much docked mass the host can move at full speed Rail Speed Controller Sets how fast rails and rotators move Rail Load / Rail Unload Moves items between a docked ship's storage and the host's Pickup Point Docks ships automatically when they come close Pickup Rail A rail meant to sit next to a Pickup Point Shootout Rail Undocks anything that moves onto it, launching it at 5× rail speed

Place a Rail Docker on your ship. Each Rail Docker shows up as a Rail Docker entry in your Weapons panel. Put it on your hotbar. Fly within 100 m of a rail on the host, aim at the rail and fire with that slot selected. You don't have to line anything up: the docker's arrow face snaps onto the rail's arrow face like a magnet, and your ship ends up one block out from the rail. Only ships can dock (not stations), and the host must be neutral, your faction, public, or a faction you are in. After a dock attempt or undocking there is a 5 second cooldown. Create Docking in the advanced build mode panel builds a new docked entity right on a rail. See Advanced Building.

Once docked, the Rail Docker entry on your hotbar is replaced by Undock. Fire with it selected to undock. You can also undock from the host: The Docks section of the structure panel has Undock All, Turrets and Normal buttons. Sending a logic signal to a docked ship's Rail Docker undocks it. A Shootout Rail at the end of a track launches ships off it.

There is no hard size or mass limit for docking. Instead, each structure can move 50 mass of docked entities at full speed, plus 50 for every Rail Mass Enhancer on it. Enhancers can go anywhere on the host; they don't need linking, but each uses some reactor power. For every unit of mass over that limit, rails, rotators and AI turret turning slow down by 5%, to a minimum of 5% speed.

A turret is built from docked entities on Rail Turret Axis blocks. One axis only rotates around one axis, so a full turret uses two: A docker facing up or down on its entity turns around the vertical axis (yaw); a docker facing sideways tilts (pitch). The turret pivots on the docker, not the ship core, so the core can go anywhere on the turret. The barrel (the last entity in the chain) does the aiming and turns the base with it. Turrets can't rotate into blocks around them, so leave them room to turn. Heavier turrets turn slower under AI control.

Put a BOBBY AI Module on the barrel (the entity on the last axis) and tick Active; it is set to the Turret type automatically. Turrets use the host's faction, so they don't need a Faction Module. From the host, , turns docked AI on and off and . resets turret rotation. See Ship & Turret AI for targeting, remote control and the rest of the AI settings.
Docked entities run on the reactor of the root ship, so turrets don't need their own reactor. While the host's shields are above 25%, they also take hits aimed at its docked entities.

For carrier hangars, place a Pickup Point next to a rail (usually a Pickup Rail): An unpiloted ship whose Rail Docker comes within 3 m of an active Pickup Point docks to the rail next to it. Your own ship does too while you fly it. The Pickup Point can be turned on and off with logic. A docked ship remembers the Pickup Point it used. The Carrier Recall fleet order sends fleet ships back to their pickup points on the flagship.

Ships docked to a Rail Basic move along the track by themselves, in the direction of the rail arrows, until the track ends. Use this for elevators, launch tubes and sliding doors. Rail Rotator Clock Wise / Counter Clock Wise: with nothing linked, it turns the docked entity 90° as it arrives. Link Activation Modules to it to set the angle: each active one adds 45°, and 9 or more make it turn non-stop. Link a Display Module with a number (0–360) to set an exact angle. Rail Speed Controller: link it to rails and rotators (C/V; Shift+V adds all touching rails), then link Activation Modules to it. Speed is the share of those modules that are on: 5 on and 5 off means 50% speed, and all off stops the track. Rails without a controller run at 50%.

Link the ship's Rail Docker to Storage blocks on the ship, and link a Rail Load or Rail Unload to Storage on the host: Rail Load moves items from the host's storage into the docked ship's storage. Rail Unload moves items from the docked ship to the host. Storage filters still apply.

A ship core makes no power of its own. Without a reactor your thrusters run at only 5% of their strength and weapons, shields and other systems don't work, so every real ship needs a reactor. This page covers the basics. See Reactors and Chambers for the details.

Reactor Power blocks make power. All reactor blocks that touch each other form one reactor, and the more blocks it has, the more power it makes. There is no special shape: any group works. A ship can have several reactors, but only one is active at a time. Inactive reactors make no power. You can switch the active reactor in the reactor menu (10 second cooldown). Reactor Stabilizer blocks keep the active reactor stable: The first 10 reactor blocks are free. After that you need one stabilizer per reactor block for 100% stability. Stabilizers can go anywhere on the ship, in as many groups as you like, at any distance from the reactor. Only your 20 biggest groups count. Below 100% stability your reactor still makes full power, but the ship takes extra damage from beams and explosions, up to 21× at 0%.

A reactor's level goes up by one for every 150 reactor blocks (0–149 blocks is level 0). The level sets how big your chambers must be: at level 0 a single chamber block is enough, and each level after that needs about 7–8 more chamber blocks per chamber.

Open the Reactor Menu with Insert, from the radial menu (Tab), or with the REACTOR button on the top bar while you are in a ship with a reactor. It shows everything about your reactors: size, level, power, stability and capacity. Use its previous/next buttons to switch the active reactor, and open the chamber tree from it.

Reactor Chambers give your ship special bonuses and abilities. Connect them to the reactor (or to each other) with Reactor Conduit blocks. Each chamber uses some Reactor Capacity (RC), and you can't go over 100%. To set up a chamber, open the reactor menu, select the unspecified chamber, press Specify Chamber, and pick an option. You can then upgrade it for a stronger effect at the cost of more RC. There are eight chamber types: Chamber What it does Defence Shield capacity, armor HP and damage-type armor FTL Jump drive (distance, autocharge), jump inhibitors, warp gates Logistics Mining bonus, faster and cheaper factories, smaller cargo volume Mass Gravity fields Mobility Top speed, turn rate, thrust blast, anti-gravity Power Reactor boost and failsafe Recon Scanners: ores, cargo, cloaked ships Stealth Cloaking, jamming, anti lock-on See Chambers for each tree.

Shipyards are Space Station based systems that allow players to design ships in a temporary virtual creative environment and mass produce those designs from a loaded design, which is similar to a blueprint. You can also dock an existing ship into a shipyard to completely deconstruct it, or repair it using an existing loaded design.

Shipyards are constructed from a Shipyard Computer, Shipyard Modules, and a Shipyard Core Anchor. The computer, as with any other system computer, must have all of the Shipyard Modules connected to it, as well as the Shipyard Core Anchor. A shipyard is only valid if the Shipyard Modules form a C shape, with both "ends" of the C being straight across from each other. A player can build as many or as few C-shaped sections as they want without affecting the function of a shipyard, provided that they are lined up. It should look something like this. The Shipyard Core Anchor can be placed anywhere within the perimeter of a Shipyard, but it is important that there are no solid blocks near it and that it is sufficiently spaced from the edges of the Shipyard to allow space for ships to take up. Note that wherever you place the Shipyard Core Anchor is where the actual Ship Core will appear. Ship designs will fail to load into the Shipyard Computer if there is not enough space inside the Shipyard Modules area for the ship.

Ships can dock to a Shipyard Core Anchor as they would with any other Rail. If they do not have a Rail Docker, the Activation Beam from a core or camera can be used to connect with the Anchor. Either way, the ship is docked with the Ship Core at the position of the Shipyard Core Anchor. The Ship Core is always docked in alignment to the Shipyard Core Anchor.

Shipyards use a special type of item called 'Designs' to function. They are similar to blueprints, and can be interchanged with blueprints through the Shipyard Computer. To create a new ship, use the Create New Design function in the Shipyard Computer. This will create a blank design with a virtual Ship Core at the position of the Shipyard Core Anchor. Blocks cannot be placed on the virtual ship except in build mode. The virtual ship is almost identical in function to a normal ship, except for a few important aspects: The virtual ship cannot be edited except in the Shipyard's build mode. The virtual ship cannot be undocked (however, use of Flight Mode without undocking is permitted, e.g. to test logic) The virtual ship has a hologram-styled shader applied to all of its blocks outside of the Shipyard's build mode. When editing the virtual ship, regardless of permissions, the player uses a Creative Mode inventory. Using blocks from a linked cargo in your inventory will not actually consume materials, rather behaving like creative mode.

The Test Sector is a virtual space in which a Design can be tested. Although it would seem to be a special Sector, it is not. It takes its surroundings from a specific location in System 0,0,0. As such, if there is a Pirate Station near that specific sector, it can cause problems when testing designs. Nominally, there would be no Pirate Stations present, and the player would be able to spawn in enemies of their choosing to fight or spawn static armored/shielded targets to test weapons on their design. It should be noted that, although it is assured that use of the Test Sector imparts no penalty on the player, death while in the Test Sector results in respawning at the player's most recently-activated Undeathinator. This can be problematic for some players who forgot to set their spawn point at their far-out base.

Assuming that all the necessary materials to construct a loaded ship design is present in the Shipyard Computer's inventory (which can be expanded with the use of Cargo), ships can be constructed, undocked, and reconstructed quickly. The Shipyard will, regardless of size, place up to 2,500 blocks per tick, meaning that a ship would have to be massive to take more than a couple minutes to be fully constructed with enough materials. Most small ships, such as drones, take only a few seconds to be constructed. In the Shipyard Computer, there is an option to undock the newly-constructed ship, so that all you have to do is move the new ship out of the way before re-loading and constructing the design again. When used properly, Shipyards can produce entire fleets of AI-controlled ships rapidly.

Shipyards can also be used to repair damaged ships or update mass-produced ships to a new standard design. This is done through a function of the Shipyard Computer, which basically deconstructs the ship and reconstructs it according to the loaded design. This design does not have to bear any resemblance to the original ship. Note that, since repairing completely deconstructs the ship and rebuilds it, it resets any saved hotbar configurations. A less destructive Ship repairing solution would be to use an Atrotech Beam instead.

The Shipyard Computer can be used to deconstruct a docked ship and save it to a design, or simply deconstruct it without saving any design. This can be used to rapidly disassemble unused AI fleets or drones.

Your character moves in two very different ways: walking where there is gravity, and floating freely in zero gravity.

Planets always have gravity. On ships and stations you need a Gravity Unit block: look at it and press R to step into its gravity field. Its gravity pulls toward the bottom of the block, so place it the way you want "down" to point. Action Key Walk W A S D Sprint Double-tap W and hold Jump Space Crouch Left Shift (hold) Prone Z (press again or Space to stand) Look Mouse Activate a block R Crouching halves your speed and lowers your view. You stay crouched while there's a low ceiling above you. Prone is very slow but keeps you low to the ground. You can't go prone while swimming, sitting or climbing. Sprint only works going forwards.

A Trigger (Area) wired through logic to a Gravity Unit switches you into that gravity field as you walk through it, so you don't have to press R at the entrance. A Gravity Exit Unit used the same way takes you out of the field again. See Logic Basics.
Walk into a Ladder block to grab it. Hold W to climb; let go and you slide back down. Press Space, S, A or D to let go of the ladder.
In water you swim in the direction you look. Space swims up, and at the surface it climbs you out. You can't sprint or go prone in water.

Outside a gravity field you float freely in all six directions. Action Key Move forward / backward W / S Strafe left / right A / D Move up / down E / Q Slow drift Left Shift (hold) Look Mouse Align to the structure in front of you Space A Thrust Pack worn in your back slot makes you much faster in zero gravity.

When you are floating near a ship or station, press Space to align to it. You then move with the structure wherever it goes. This is very useful for: Moving around inside a piloted or AI-controlled ship without getting bashed into walls or left behind entirely when it moves Fitting through small doors, hallways, and vertical shafts which may only accommodate a character facing the right direction Placing blocks with the proper orientation as an astronaut (the build preview [CTRL] updates its orientation with your alignment) To let go, press Space again while not looking at the structure. If it is moving fast, the game asks you to confirm first.

Magnetic Boots, worn in your feet slot, let you stand on any surface: ships, stations and planets, including walls, ceilings and cliff faces, with no gravity module needed. Press ` while looking at a surface within reach to stand on it. Press it at another surface to move onto that one. Press it while looking at nothing to let go. In zero gravity, Space (Align) also locks the boots on. To wear gear, drag it into its slot on the Equipment tab of your inventory.

In build mode, movement is the same as zero gravity, but you pass through blocks. Hold Left Shift to move much faster around large ships. Mining is done with a ship's salvage beam, not by hand. See Resources & Mining.
The HUD (Heads-Up Display) gives you live information about your character and ship at a glance.

On foot you see: Crosshair in the centre of the screen. Hotbar at the bottom, with your health bar (green) just above it. Radar in the top-right corner, with your current sector coordinates below it. Use these when setting navigation waypoints. Target panel in the top-left corner while you have something selected (F selects what you are looking at). On a planet, a location readout under the radar adds your position on the planet, altitude, biome, time of day and the current weather.

When you fly a ship, bars curve around the crosshair: Side Bar What it shows Left Shield (yellow) Shield charge Left Armor / Structure Armor HP and structure HP Right Power (blue) Reactor power: what you have against what your systems are drawing Right Speed (white) Current speed Right Heat Heat from cannon and beam fire. Heat Sink blocks soak it up; once they are full, those weapons can't fire until it cools. Buffs (green) and debuffs (red) from weapon effects show up near the centre of the screen. A flash on the crosshair tells you what you hit: blue for shields, white for blocks, red for a character.

Ten slots mapped to keys 1–9 and 0. The mouse wheel cycles slots (except in advanced build mode). On a slot with several block shapes, the wheel steps through those first. Holds: Items and blocks (astronaut mode) Weapons and systems (ship flight mode) Blocks to place (build mode)

StarMade is a voxel-based space sandbox game. You explore a procedurally generated universe, build ships and stations block by block, gather resources, craft items, fight enemies, and team up with other players.
The universe is divided into Sectors and Systems. Pirates and other NPC Factions appear across the galaxy map. Planets and asteroids gather around star systems, waiting to be discovered.

Explore — fly through space, discover planets, asteroids, and trading stations Mine — collect raw ores and crystal shards from asteroids and planet surfaces Craft — refine materials into components and build blocks Build — construct and upgrade ships and stations Survive — defend yourself against pirates and rival players
You host your own universe. All admin commands are available. Blueprints are saved to the blueprints/ folder of your StarMade install.
You connect to a shared server. Server rules govern the gameplay style, admin command access, and may restrict builds. Blueprints saved to a server are stored server-side.

When you first spawn, you will be a humanoid Astronaut, equipped with a few tools for survival & some basic blocks to build your first Ship and fly out into the universe. The spawn location is configured by the server; by default it is sector 2, 2, 2, home to a Trading Guild Trade Station where you can buy basic supplies. Your immediate goals: Get comfortable with character movement Familiarise yourself with the HUD Learn basic controls Build your first ship Find some asteroids and mine your first resources using Salvage Beams Tip: Check the navigation panel (N by default) to locate nearby trading stations, asteroids, and planets from your starting position.
StarMade has a fully integrated, Turing-complete logic system. You can build anything from a simple light switch to a fully functional CPU using logic blocks connected to each other.
Every logic block outputs one of two states: ON or OFF. These states propagate through connections to other blocks.

The most important block in the logic system is the Activation Block. It acts as both a switch and a signal carrier. Press R on it to manually toggle it ON or OFF. When ON, it sends an ON signal to every block connected to it. When OFF, it sends an OFF signal (or no signal) to connected blocks. Activation blocks can be linked to: Other activation blocks Doors Lights Weapon computers (fire/stop) Gravity modules And any other activatable block

All logic connections use the same two-step process: Step Key Action 1 C Select the block that will send the signal 2 V Connect the selected block to the block that will receive the signal A visual indicator (coloured box) appears on connected blocks to show the connection. To remove a connection, select the source block with C again and then press V on the connection target while it is already connected.

You can create chains — activation block A → activation block B → light. When A is toggled, B receives the signal and passes it to the light. This lets you build remote switching panels, interlocked doors, and complex trigger sequences from a single input.

Linking an activation block to a weapon computer fires that weapon while the activation block is ON, and stops it when OFF. This enables: Automated firing sequences Logic-triggered turrets Shoot-when-condition-met circuits

Activation blocks can be linked directly to Gravity Modules to toggle gravity on or off. Note: the activation block must currently be directly connected to the gravity module (not through intermediate blocks).

The Command Module block lets you send pre-configured commands to other systems on your ship or station. Unlike activation blocks (which only send ON/OFF signals), command modules execute specific actions like switching reactor configurations, toggling AI modes, or controlling shipyard operations.

Place a Command Module block. Connect it to a supported target block using C (on the command module) then V (on the target). Press R on the command module to open its interface and configure the command. Select a command type and set any required parameters. Click Execute to run it manually, or trigger it via a logic signal. When triggered by logic, there is a 500 ms cooldown between executions to prevent spam.

Bobby AI Module​ Command Effect Toggle AI Flip AI on/off Activate AI Explicitly set AI on or off Target Type Set what the AI targets: Any, Selected Target, Stations, Ships, Missiles, Astronauts, Asteroids Type Set AI behavior: Ship, Fleet, Turret Reactor​ Command Effect Set Active Reactor Switch to a specific reactor tree by ID Next Reactor Cycle to the next reactor Previous Reactor Cycle to the previous reactor Reboot Reactor Reboot the active reactor Shipyard Computer​ Command Effect Create New Design Start a new shipyard design Load Design Load an existing design Unload Design Unload the current design Spawn Design Build the loaded design as a new ship Deconstruct Deconstruct a docked ship into a design Deconstruct & Recycle Deconstruct and recycle materials Catalog to Design Convert a catalog blueprint to a design Blueprint to Design Convert a blueprint to a design Design to Blueprint Save a design as a blueprint Repair from Design Repair a structure using its design as a template Warp Gate Computer​ Command Effect Set Target Sector Set the warp destination coordinates Activate Turn the gate on or off Toggle Flip the gate state Rail-Docked Entities (Turrets, etc.)​ Any block that can dock to a rail can be controlled: Command Effect Activate AI Set docked entity AI on or off Toggle AI Flip docked entity AI state Set Powered Control power transfer to the docked entity Toggle Powered Flip power transfer state Reset Rail Reset turret to its default position and rotation

Automated turret control — logic circuit detects an enemy, command module activates turret AI and sets targeting mode. Reactor switching — a button on the bridge cycles between combat and travel reactor configurations. Shipyard automation — logic triggers spawn a design when resources are ready. Warp gate networks — command modules set destination coordinates before activating the gate.

Connections are not affected by distance — a block on one end of your ship can control something on the other end. You can connect one source block to many targets — useful for turning on all lights at once. Multiple sources can connect to the same target block. Connections survive reloads and blueprint saves (if both blocks are included in the blueprint). For more complex logic (NOT, AND, OR, DELAY gates), see Logic: Gates.
Building on the basics of activation blocks and connections, StarMade provides four additional logic blocks that let you build complex circuits.

Block Behaviour NOT Inverts the input signal AND ON only when ALL inputs are ON OR ON when ANY input is ON DELAY Passes the signal with a time delay All gate blocks are connected the same way as activation blocks: C to select a source, V to connect to a destination.
The NOT block inverts its input. Common use: Keep a system running by default and shut it off when a condition is met, rather than turning it on.
The AND block outputs ON only when every single connected input is ON. Common use: A door that only opens when two independent conditions are both met (e.g. a switch AND a timer).
The OR block outputs ON when at least one connected input is ON. Common use: A system that activates from multiple independent triggers (e.g. two different switches can each open the same door).

The DELAY block passes its input signal through after a configurable time delay. Key capability: Loops. By linking a DELAY block and a NOT block into a loop, you create a clock — a continuously oscillating signal. Clocks are the foundation of: Repeating firing sequences Animated light patterns Timer-based mechanisms Complex synchronised systems

Gates can be chained and combined freely. Inputs and outputs of one gate become inputs to another. Since the system is Turing-complete, any digital logic circuit you can design on paper can be built in StarMade.
[Button A] ─┐ AND ──► [Inner Door] [Pressure] ─┘ [Button A] ──► NOT ──► [Outer Door] Both the inner and outer doors are managed so they never open at the same time.
For further study on logic gate designs, search for "logic gate truth tables" or "digital electronics basics" online. The same principles apply directly to StarMade's system.
StarMade's crafting system is divided into three basic stages: refining, component manufacturing, and block assembly.

Raw materials you mine or extract from the universe around you, must first be refined in order to be useful for further crafting. Refining transforms raw materials into blocks of Metal Mesh, Crystal Composite, and Capsules of pure material depending on the type of ore being refined. These are then used in all other manufacturing processes to create blocks used in ships, stations, and more. As its name suggests, the Basic Capsule Refinery block is the standard way to achieve this. See the "Factories" page for more information. In order to use the Basic Capsule Refinery, simply place it down, build a Reactor on the same entity to supply power, activate the refinery, and place your raw materials in its internal inventory. Like all factories, the refinery can be selected and linked to Cargo Storage to increase its internal capacity, and Factory Enhancers to increase the amount of items refined per cycle, at the cost of higher power consumption. Some naturally-occurring blocks, such as water, ice, lava, dirt, plants, and planetary rocks, are 'refined' via the Block Recycler instead.

Once you have a supply of refined materials, the next step is to transform them into useful Components. Components are pieces such as sturdy frames and advanced circuitry, that comprise the various blocks you can build with. The Component Assembler factory is the primary means to produce Components from their constituent raw materials. Components with an orange background are "Tier 1" components. They are made from Metal Mesh, Crystal Composite, and/or natural materials. Most basic blocks such as power, thrust, & salvage beams can be produced using only these ubiquitous components. Components with a blue background are "Tier 2" components. These more advanced components are manufactured using specialized material capsules. Blocks can also be broken down into their constituent Components via the Block Recycler factory.

Components can be assembled into blocks by several means. The most basic way to do this is using the Block Assembler, a factory that combines components into individual blocks. The "Change Production" button allows you to specify which block to create. Shipyard Schematics and Blueprints can also be filled out using Components in order to build pre-designed ships and structures directly.

If you find yourself stranded on an alien planet, or you forgot to obtain factories before starting up a new base, fear not! Your Space Suit includes compact personal fabricators capable of breaking down most natural ores and creating the factory blocks you need in order to get started. These fabricators are accessible via the Inventory window in your HUD. To begin, find & harvest any Metal and Crystal ores and place them in your personal refinery. Do keep in mind that, in exchange for portability, the conversion efficiency of these factory systems is lower than their standalone block equivalents.
Production or 'crafting' in StarMade is primarily achieved via various types of Factories. A full production line requires multiple linked factories.

Basic Capsule Refinery: Produces mesh/composite from basic ores, and refined resource Capsules from uncommon ores. Catalytic Capsule Refinery: Consumes Catalyst items to refine ores more efficiently than the Basic Refinery. Catalysts require extremely rare resources to manufacture.

Component Fabricator: Produces any Component from Capsules/Mesh/Composite. Block Assembler: Creates blocks from Components. Chemical Factory: Produces Catalysts from ultra rare resources for enhanced refining in the Catalytic Capsule Refinery. (In future versions of StarMade, the Chemical Factory will also produce other intermediate products for efficient specialized refining and Component production.) Shipyard: Produces Ships matching provided blueprints or existing ships, deconstructs existing ships back into their constituent parts, or allows you to create new designs without spending blocks and then produce ships from those designs later.

Block Recycler: Reclaims the constituent Components from any Block placed inside it. Micro Reprocessor: Transforms decayed scrap materials, as well as advanced metals and crystals, into basic Metal Mesh and Crystal Composite used by the Compoenet Fabricator.

Factories can only be placed on a station or a planet - they cannot be placed on ships. Factories require power to operate. You can supply power by: Shooting the factory with a personal power beam Placing a group of Reactor Power blocks on the same entity as the factory to generate power.

Press R on the factory to open its interface. Click Change Production. Use the search filter to find the item you want to produce (e.g. type "reactor" to find Reactor Power Module). Select the item from the dropdown. Click View Graph to see the full crafting tree for that item.
The View Graph button shows the entire crafting tree as a flowchart. The factory only processes the topmost step — everything below it must be handled by separate factories.

[Power Reactor Module] ← your Block Assembler produces this ├─ [Structural Frame] ← a Component Fabricator must provide this │ └─ [Metal Mesh] ← a Capsule Refinery/Micro Reprocessor provides this └─ [Energy Cell] ← a Component Fabricator must provide this ├─ [Metal Mesh] └─ [Crystal Composite] Your Block Assembler factory takes the Structural Frame and Energy Cell components as inputs, and outputs Power Reactor Modules. You need additional factories set up to produce each of those, which in turn must be supplied raw materials from a Refinery factory.

Factories can pull ingredients from other Factories or Storages automatically using connections: Press C on the factory that needs to be supplied with items. Press V on the factory or storage block that produces or holds those items. The first factory will now draw needed materials from the second automatically. With a properly linked chain, you place raw materials into the bottom factory and the top factory outputs the final product — everything in between is handled automatically.

By default, factories can only process one item at a time. If you plan on building a mighty star cruiser to conquer the universe, this is extremely slow! Factory Enhancers are extremely useful blocks that allow you to batch-process multiples of an item at once using a single Factory. Each Factory Enhancer represents one extra item/block your Factory can produce at once. Pressing C on the factory and V on a Factory Enhancer links it to the factory. Shift+V can link entire groups of enhancers at once. Only one Factory can make use of any given Factory Enhancer block(s) at a time. If you have a heavily-enhanced factory but only need 1 of something, you can set a production limit in the factory's UI panel.

The Factory Manager block automates an entire production chain. Instead of manually setting recipes and linking factories one by one, a Factory Manager analyzes what needs to be built, figures out what raw materials are missing, and assigns recipes to connected factories automatically.

Place a Factory Manager on your station. Connect it to your factories — link the Factory Manager to every factory you want it to control using C (on the manager) and V (on each factory). It supports all factory types. Connect it to storage — link the Factory Manager to inventories (storage blocks) so it can see what raw materials are available. Place an order — tell the manager what you want produced. Orders can come from: A factory — the manager reads what recipe is set and ensures all intermediate ingredients are produced. A shipyard — the manager produces all blocks needed for a ship under construction. A storage filter — the manager keeps a storage filled to the quantities defined in its filter.

When an order is placed, the Factory Manager: Walks the crafting tree — starting from the requested item, it recursively determines every intermediate product and raw material needed. Checks inventories — it scans connected storage to see what materials are already available and reserves them. Identifies shortages — any raw material that no connected factory can produce is added to a shopping list (materials the player must supply). Prioritizes production — items are sorted by urgency. Bottleneck ingredients (ones blocking other production steps) are prioritized over items already in surplus. Assigns recipes to factories — the manager sets each connected factory's recipe and production limit automatically, activating idle factories and shutting down ones with nothing to produce.

The Factory Manager accounts for the capability of each factory (based on the amount of Factory Enhancers linked to the given factory block). When deciding how much to produce per cycle, it estimates combined capacity as roughly the sum of all factory capabilities of a given type, ensuring larger factories are assigned work first.

The Factory Manager tracks two resource lists: Needed (remaining) — raw materials still required to complete the current order. Total — all raw materials the full order requires from the start. Both lists can be copied to the clipboard directly from the Factory Manager interface, making it easy to see exactly what you need to gather.

When viewing the crafting graph through a Factory Manager, nodes are color-coded: Color Meaning Green Resource is fully stocked Blue Resource is partially available Red Resource is missing or insufficient

Power matters. A factory without power stalls. Build a sufficiently large reactor in order to supply your factory. Use View Graph every time you set up a new production line — it clearly shows exactly what inputs the factory expects at each step. Multiple factories can be linked to one source factory — the source will supply whatever any of its connected factories need. Use a Factory Manager for complex production chains — it eliminates the tedious manual setup of recipe assignment and linking, especially when producing blocks that require many intermediate steps. Reduce, reuse, recycle! All blocks are made from a small selection of common Components. If you have spare blocks from a previous building project, salvage mission, or loot from combat, they may be a gold mine in disguise! Try disassembling leftover blocks in the Block Recycler and see if they provide the necessary Components for your new project, before running off on a mining trip for fresh resources.
The Catalog stores ship blueprints — saved snapshots of ships and stations that can be purchased and spawned elsewhere.
Open your inventory (I) and click the Catalog tab, or press U in build mode.
While inside the ship you want to save: Open the Catalog. Click Create New Entry. The ship is saved as a blueprint.

Server admins and singleplayer players can use chat commands: /save <name> — saves your current ship or the last ship you were in /load <name> — loads (spawns) a blueprint by name Stations saved via /save are not listed in the Catalog but can be loaded with /load.

Catalog Where blueprints are stored When used Server Catalog Server's blueprints/ folder Default; visible to all on that server Local Catalog Your StarMade/blueprints/ folder on your PC Singleplayer; private to you In multiplayer, tick Save in Local Catalog when saving if you want to keep the blueprint private on your machine rather than uploading it to the server.

You can upload a blueprint from your local catalog to the server so you can spawn it there: In the Catalog, find the local blueprint. Click Upload to Server. The server owner and admins will also have access to uploaded blueprints. Only upload designs you are comfortable sharing.
documents.s: Uploading Local Blueprints to a Server

documents.t: Each catalog entry has a permission level controlling who can spawn it: Permission Who can spawn Others Anyone Faction Only your faction members Homebase Only from your faction's homebase Enemy Usable Also available for pirates and NPCs (admin/singleplayer only)

At any shop you can purchase and spawn a blueprint: Approach a shop. Open the Catalog tab. Find the blueprint and click Buy / Spawn. The game checks if you have the required blocks in your inventory. If you have the blocks, the ship spawns. Blueprints are essentially "recipes" — the game deducts the required blocks from your inventory each time you spawn one. The design is saved permanently; you can spawn it as many times as you can afford the materials.

Local blueprints are stored in your StarMade/blueprints/ folder as .sment files. You can: Copy them to another computer Share them with friends Upload them to multiplayer servers This makes it possible to build a design in singleplayer, perfect it, then deploy it on a multiplayer server.
Factions let players group together, protect their ships and stations, declare wars, and organise with ranks and permissions.

Press H to open the Faction Panel. Tab Purpose Personal Create a new faction or manage your current membership Faction Edit your faction's description, news, and diplomacy Faction Hub Browse all factions on the server; join public ones Invites Accept pending invitations To create a faction: go to the Personal tab → Create New Faction → enter a name → OK. To join: find a public faction in the Faction Hub and click join, or accept an invitation in the Invites tab.

In the Faction tab → options: Option Effect Public Faction Anyone can join without an invitation Declare War on Hostile Action Auto-declares war if your faction is attacked Consider Neutral Enemy Treats all factionless entities as enemies
Every member has a rank. Ranks are configurable with custom names and permission sets. Click Roles in the Faction tab to manage them.

Permission Grants Edit Can edit faction description and post news Kick Can kick members of lower rank Invite Can invite new players Permission-Edit Can modify rank permissions — give only to trusted leaders To change a member's rank: click Options next to their name → select a rank.

From the Faction Hub tab, click the Relation button next to any other faction to: Declare war Send a peace offer Send an alliance offer Peace and alliance offers must be accepted by the other faction's leaders.
You can declare war against a single player rather than their whole faction. In the Faction tab → Personal Enemies.

To assign a ship or station to your faction: Place a Faction Module on the structure. Press R on it. Enter your faction signature (visible in the faction panel). While the faction module exists and is not destroyed, only you and your faction members can use that structure.

documents.t: A station claimed by a faction can be designated as the faction's Homebase (only one per faction). The homebase has a major advantage: The homebase and everything docked to it are invulnerable to damage. This makes the homebase the safest location for your most valuable assets. Choose its location and defences carefully — it is the heart of your faction.
Send messages only to faction members by typing /f before your message in chat.
Understanding armor and damage types is essential for both building durable ships and designing effective weapons.

All damage in StarMade is split across three types: Type Description Kinetic Physical impact; most effective against unarmored system blocks Heat Thermal damage; most effective against armored hull blocks EM Electromagnetic; most effective against shields Different weapons deal different mixes of these types. The Damage Beam, for example, is heavily EM (≈50% EM, ≈33% Heat, ≈17% Kinetic), making it more effective against shield-heavy targets. Effect blocks connected to a weapon computer can shift its damage type distribution. Systems, armor, and shields each have one heavy resistance, one slight resistance, and one damage type with no resistance. Type Kinetic Resistance Heat Resistance EM Resistance Systems 0% 15% 10% Armor 10% 0 % 15% Shields 15% 10% 0%

Basic Armor blocks provide structural protection. They come in multiple colours (Grey, White, Dark Grey, Black, and many more) and shapes (full block, wedge, corner, hepta, tetra, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 slab) for hull construction. All armour colors and shapes have the same combat stats per block; the shape variants are purely for aesthetics and hull smoothing. Standard Armor and Advanced Armor offer greater armor value per block but are heavier and more expensive to craft. Advanced Armor has lower total HP, but much higher armor value, making it stronger overall. Type HP Armor Value Mass Basic 200 0.1 0.05 Standard 300 4.4 0.1 Advanced 150 15.63 0.2

Armor uses an exponential formula to determine how much damage passes through: Damage dealt = D² / (A³ + D) Where D = incoming damage per shot and A = total armor value in the path of the shot. Armor thickness is only calculated up to 32 blocks, but thicker armor is still more durable as it can maintain a 32 block thickness even as outer layers of the hull are destroyed. Overpenetration occurs when a cannon hit does more than 20 times an armor block's HP before accounting for reduction by armor value. When overpenetrating, the cannon shell will pass straight through the block instead of stopping and spreading damage to all surrounding blocks. Overpenetration does not apply to damage beams and missiles.

Every armor block on a ship (or station, or planet...) contributes to the structure's pool of Armor Hit Points, or AHP. While AHP remains above zero, heavy armor will be even tougher, and the extra damage absorbed will be incurred as AHP damage rather than block destruction. The effect of AHP is a multiplier of the effect of armor thickness, so thin armor will still be easier to break through than thick armor even if a ship has some or all AHP remaining.

Just as with shields, armor's damage reduction mechanics are bypassed by bombs (the Missile/Missile combo weapon). They are a high-risk, high-reward weapon which is relatively easy for an agile ship to avoid, however a heavy and slow armored ship may be vulnerable to bombers. Bomb damage is still absorbed by raw block hitpoints, however, so Basic and Standard Armor, with their higher hitpoints per weight, are likely the most efficient way to 'soak up' bomb explosions before the blast wave can reach critical systems.

Small hits are almost completely absorbed by substantial armor. A wall of armor is nearly impenetrable against many weak shots. Massive single cannon hits penetrate. A cannon shot doing more than 20× the armor block's HP bypasses it entirely via overpenetration. Situation Best approach Defending against many small rapid-fire hits Thick armor wall; Machine gun and sustained beams struggle Defending against high-damage burst weapons Harder to block; armor is penetrated by high damage Attacking armored ships Use high-damage burst combos (Charge Cannon, Sniper Cannon) to reach overpenetration threshold Attacking unarmored ships Any weapon combo works; shields are the main barrier; focus on EM damage

Linking effect blocks to a weapon computer shifts the weapon's Kinetic/Heat/EM distribution. Different armor tiers and special block types may have varying resistances to each damage type — this is exposed in the block properties panel in build mode. Effect block combinations and exact resistances are configurable on servers and may vary.

documents.t: Ships are built block by block in Build Mode. This guide takes you through spawning your first ship and making it flight-ready.

Press X (default: Spawn Ship) to place a new Ship Core block in the world. Give your ship a name when prompted. The core must have enough clear space around it to materialise. Tip: Don't look at the ground or a wall when spawning — the core needs room in the direction you are facing. After spawning, enter the ship with R (look at the core first), then switch to build mode with Z.

In build mode you pass through all blocks and float freely. This makes it easy to work inside and around your ship. Action Key Place block Left Mouse Button Remove block Right Mouse Button Select block 1–9, 0 / Mouse wheel Fast movement Left Shift (hold) Advanced Build Mode Left Ctrl (hold) Build tools radial menu ` Undo Ctrl+Z The selected block type is shown in your hotbar. Open your inventory (I) to move blocks into the hotbar slots.

A bare ship core cannot move or fire weapons. At minimum you need: Power Reactor Module — place one or more anywhere on the ship. More reactor blocks = more power generation. A Reactor system's blocks must be in one contiguous group (see Ship Systems). Thruster Module — place one or more anywhere on the ship. More thruster blocks = more top speed and acceleration. The direction the thrusters face doesn't matter mechanically — they all provide thrust force in all directions. The Thruster Menu can be used to distribute thrust strength differently along different axes. With both a Reactor and some Thrusters placed, switch to flight mode (Z) — you can now fly.

To arm your ship: Place a Weapon Computer block (e.g. Cannon Computer). Place several Weapon Barrel/Module blocks near it. These are the actual gun barrels. Open the Weapon Panel (G). Drag the weapon computer into a hotbar slot at the bottom of the panel. Close the panel and select that slot with the number keys. The weapon computer turns orange and pulses when it is the last selected/placed computer — this indicates it is "active" for connections. See Weapons for details on weapon types and combinations.

At any time, you can save your current ship as a blueprint: Open the Catalog (U, or the Catalog tab in inventory) Click Create New Entry The blueprint is saved and can later be spawned at any shop, provided you supply the required blocks See Catalog & Blueprints for the full catalog guide.

Build symmetrically — symmetrical builds are faster and easier to keep visually balanced. Use symmetry planes (see Advanced Building) to mirror blocks automatically. Protect your reactor — the reactor is your ship's most critical system. Surround it with other systems, hull, and armour. Protect systems computers — a destroyed weapon computer block disables that entire weapon system. Use build mode fast movement (Left Shift) to move quickly around large ships.

Chambers are special blocks that plug into your reactor to give your ship additional capabilities — jump drives, stealth, enhanced mobility, and more. They are the primary way to unlock advanced ship systems.

Chambers must be physically connected to the reactor using Reactor Conduit blocks. A chain of conduits running from a chamber back to a Reactor Block completes the connection. The conduit chain can be any length and can route around other blocks — it just needs to form a continuous connected path from the chamber back to a Reactor Block.

Each reactor has a chamber capacity budget that remains fixed, regardless of the size of the reactor. Each chamber you install costs a portion of that budget. You cannot exceed 100% capacity. Monitor your capacity usage in the ship stats panel.

Chamber Effect Mobility Upgrades ship movement speed and agility Jump Upgrades a ship's Jump Drive system Stealth Enhances a ship's Stealth system functionality, such as allowing full invisibility or longer stealth durations Recon Enhances scan range and detection ability Logistics Improves cargo and logistics handling

In build mode, place one or more Reactor Conduit blocks forming a path from a Reactor Block or parent Chamber outward. Place the Chamber Block at the end of the conduit path (touching the last conduit). The chamber activates automatically when the connection is valid. Tip: Give each base chamber its own conduit line to a Reactor Block. A conduit between two chambers makes the second one an upgrade of the first, so it can only be specified from the first chamber's tree.
Every ship needs a power reactor to run its systems. This guide covers how to build and balance your reactor.

Block Role Reactor Power Generates power. More blocks = more power regen and a higher reactor level. Reactor Stabilizer Keeps the reactor stable. Below 100% stability the ship takes extra damage. Reactor Conduit Connects chambers to the reactor (see Chambers).

Reactor Power blocks that touch each other form one reactor. Its power regen increases with every block in it. A ship can hold more than one reactor, but only one is active at a time. You can switch the active reactor from the reactor panel; switching has a 10 second cooldown.

Stability compares your stabilizers to the size of your active reactor: stability = (10 + stabilizers) ÷ reactor blocks, capped at 100% The first 10 reactor blocks are stabilized for free. After that, you need one stabilizer per reactor block. Stabilizers can go anywhere on the ship — distance and direction from the reactor don't matter. Only your 20 largest stabilizer groups count, so don't scatter them as single blocks all over the hull. Stability does not reduce your power output, but below 100% your ship takes extra damage from beams and explosions (missiles and explosive effects). Cannon hits are not affected. Stability Damage taken 100% Normal 90% About 3× 50% About 11× 0% 21× Tip: Always aim for 100% stability. You can check it in the ship's reactor panel. Losing stabilizers in combat lowers it, so a few spare stabilizers buy you margin.

Reactor level goes up by one for every 150 reactor blocks (0–149 blocks is level 0, 150 is level 1, 300 is level 2, and so on). Level matters because it sets how many chamber blocks you need to activate chambers (see Chambers). It is also shown in the flight HUD when you select a ship (F), so you can quickly size up a potential adversary by its reactor level.

Your systems draw power continuously, and more while they charge. If the reactor can't keep up, weapons and other charged systems recharge more slowly, and once they get less than 90% of the power they need at rest they start to lose charge. When the active reactor loses blocks, it starts rebooting: for at least 15 seconds (longer the more damaged the reactor and the heavier the ship) you can't place reactor or chamber blocks or change your chambers.
Salvagers function similarly to weapons, but without secondaries or effects. Salvage systems are used to mine ores from asteroids, and to salvage overheating shipwrecks and abandoned stations.

Every weapon system consists of at least two block types: Salvage Computer — The controller. Assign it to a hotbar slot. One per salvager system. Salvage Beam Modules — The actual firepower. More modules = more power. (Optional) Storage — Link a storage block to the salvage computer to have the mined blocks go to the storage instead of your limited personal inventory.

Larger groups of salvage modules can salvage multiple blocks at once. For each doubling of salvage modules in a group, the radius salvaged increases by 1, starting with a radius of 1 at 8 modules in a group, and scaling up to a maximal radius of 10 at 4096 modules.

Shields are your ship's first layer of defence. All incoming damage hits shields before reaching your hull and blocks. When shields are depleted they enter a Shield Outage before recharging. Damage Hits Shields First Incoming damage SHIELDS ARMOR SYSTEMS When shields are depleted they enter an outage; hits then pass to armor, then internal systems.

Shield Rechargers convert Reactor Power into Shields, which are stored by Shield Capacitors inside their Shield Radius. Each block contributes more hitpoints per second, but costs. The total stats of a Shield system are visible in the Build Mode UI. This Reactor Power cost does not change whether the Shield Rechargers are resting or actively charging. Shield Radius (the zone around your ship that the shield covers) projects from the center of each contiguous group of Shield Rechargers, and scales up with block count on an exponential curve — small ships get good coverage quickly; large ships need proportionally more blocks for full hull coverage. It is not a "shield bubble"; The shield is skin-tight to the hull of the ship, and the Shield Radius just shows what part of the hull is covered. Each contiguous group of Shield Rechargers produces its own Shield Radius. If the center of one Shield Radius is inside another Shield Radius, the smaller of the two will be disabled. Shield Radius determines which which Capacity Banks are charged by which Shield Recharger group. To be charged, a Capacity Bank must be inside the Shield Recharger group's Shield Radius. Each Capacity Bank can only belong to one Shield Recharger group, so in the event of Shield Radius overlap, the Capacity Bank will go to the largest Shield Recharger group. Capacity Bank ownership is indicated by pink arrows from the center of the Capacity Bank to the center of the Shield Recharger group.
documents.s: Shield Recharger Blocks and Shield Radius

documents.t: Place Shield Capacitor blocks on your ship to add shield capacity to the nearby shield system. As stated above, Shield Capacitor groups must be placed within a Shield Recharger system's radius in order to contribute hitpoints to the shield system. Every contiguous group of Shield Capacitors forms a Capacity Bank. A single shield system can only have up to 20 Capacity Banks, so make sure your Shield Capacitors are grouped together to avoid going over the limit.

Shield Capacitors slowly 'leak' away stored shield HP if not replenished constantly. Each point of Shield Capacity requires 0.004 points of Shield Upkeep per second. This equates to 1 point per block of Shield Capacitors. If Shield Recharge is less than the Shield Upkeep cost, the shield system will drain itself until it reaches zero HP.

A Shield Recharger group that has not taken any damage for the last 1 minute will recharge at its full rate regardless of how much Shield Capacity the group currently has. Shield Under Fire is a debuff that lasts for 1 minute after a Shield Recharger group has taken Shield damage. During this time, Shield Recharge is reduced, from a 0% reduction at 100% Shield Capacity to a 50% reduction at 20% Shield Capacity. The amount of reduction is based on the lowest percentage the Shield Recharger group reached while afflicted with the debuff, rather than the current Shield Capacity. Shield Outage is a debuff that lasts for 10 seconds after a Shield Recharger group has reached 0% Shield Capacity. During this time, Shield Recharge for this group is completely disabled.
Turrets and docked ships have their shields disabled while they are docked. When they are hit by weapons, they will be protected by the shields of the ship or station they are docked to instead.

Shield-related chamber trees can boost: Total capacity (more buffer before breaking) Shield upkeep (less shield upkeep cost) Recovery time (shorter lockout after shield break) See the Chambers guide for details.

While it is possible to have multiple groups of Shield Rechargers on one ship, it is almost always better to have a single group that covers all of the ship when possible. It's important to make sure you have enough Shield Regen to still regenerate while afflicted with the Shield Under Fire debuff. If your Shield Upkeep exceeds your Shield Regen you will rapidly lose your shields and start taking hull damage.
A ship, station turret or docked entity with a BOBBY AI Module can fly and fight on its own. Only one AI Module is allowed per ship.

Place a BOBBY AI Module on the ship. Press R on it to open the AI panel. You can also press ; (or the AI button on the top bar) while you are in the ship. Pick a Type and tick Active. Entering a ship's core or a cockpit turns its AI off. Turn it back on when you leave. The AI also switches off if the ship's core overheats. A logic signal into the AI Module turns the AI on or off.

Type What it does Ship Hunts enemies within 3 sectors, flies to them and fights Turret Stays docked, turns to face targets in weapon range and fires Fleet Waits for orders from its fleet. See Fleets The game picks some of these for you: An entity docked on the last axis of a turret becomes a Turret. See Docking & Turrets. A ship that joins a fleet becomes Fleet and turns on; when it leaves the fleet it goes back to Ship.

The AI attacks whoever its faction is at war with. Pirates are enemies of everyone. A ship without a faction only fights Pirates (and other factions that attack neutrals). Docked turrets without their own faction use the host's faction. The AI never targets shops, cloaked ships, or anything in a protected sector. When a Ship AI is hit by an enemy, it turns on the attacker (at most once every 25 seconds).

Setting What it does Active Turns the AI on or off Type Ship, Turret or Fleet Remote Control Turrets only: lets the host's pilot aim the turrets (see below) Priority How to choose between targets: Random, Closest, Furthest, Weakest, Strongest, Lightest, Heaviest, Lowest shields, Highest shields Keep target until lost Stay on one target instead of picking again every scan Minimum range Ship AI: the distance to keep from its target. Auto fights up close Maximum range Ship AI: how far away it fights from. It can't be more than the range of your weapons. Auto uses your weapon range Multi-Output Fire Mode Volley makes every cannon and missile fire in volleys; Simultaneous leaves each weapon's own setting Missile Damage Prioritization Shown when Missiles is first in Aim At: shoot the missiles with the Highest or Lowest damage first, or Random

An ordered list of what turrets shoot at: Selected Target, Ships, Stations, Missiles, Astronauts and Asteroids. Turn each one on or off and move it up or down; the turret goes for the first kind it finds. New AIs aim at Ships, Stations and Astronauts. Selected Target: the target the host's pilot has pinned for the AI (X while flying), or the host AI's own target. Missiles: point defence. Turrets shoot down enemy missiles in range. Asteroids: a turret with salvage beams mines nearby asteroids.

Pick which systems the AI shoots at on its target, in priority order: Reactors, Stabilizers, Chambers, Thrusters, Shield Rechargers, Shield Capacitors. With focus fire off, the AI aims at a random system on the target.

It flies to the target and stops a bit inside its weapon range (or at its Minimum range), then circles while firing. Against targets on a planet it makes strafing runs instead: dive, fire, pull up and turn back for another pass. A ship armed with only warheads rams its target. It steers around other ships and gas giants in its way. When it loses its target it stays where it is and searches again every few seconds. It doesn't flee, patrol or go home. Out of combat it uses its scanner; in combat it uses cloaking, jamming and jump inhibitors if it has them. With no thrusters it barely moves.

Turrets only look for targets within their weapon range. The range sliders don't affect them. Turrets lead moving targets (except beam-only turrets). After 30 seconds without a target, a turret turns back to its starting rotation.

With Remote Control on, the pilot of the host ship can select Turret Control on the hotbar. The turrets then aim wherever the pilot looks and fire when they click. With another slot selected, the turrets go back to picking their own targets.
Cannons, beams and missiles linked to the core. It switches between them every half second. Repair beams on friendly ships that are damaged. Salvage beams on asteroids.
